tier_reason: Paper sec. 5 states GCC 5.4, -O3 -march=native, Intel i7-6700 (Skylake), and the benchmark code is public at github.com/RoaringBitmap/CBitmapCompetition (src/roaring_benchmarks.c, src/bitset_benchmarks.c, src/stl_vector_benchmarks.cpp, src/stl_hashset_benchmarks.cpp); it benchmarks the compiler's own C++ standard library containers (std::vector, std::unordered_set) as well as an uncompressed bitset.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Mixed by dataset and operation (CPU cycles per input value, Tables 4/6/7). vs C++ standard library containers: two-by-two intersections (Table 7a), sorted std::vector + std::set_intersection 7.84 vs Roaring 0.220 on CensusInc (~36x, derived from page data), 3.28 vs 0.090 on Census1881 (~36x, derived from page data), 4.15 vs 1.43 on Wikileaks (~2.9x, derived from page data); std::unordered_set 55.3 vs 0.220 on CensusInc (~251x, derived from page data), 0.480 vs 0.090 on Census1881 (~5.3x, derived from page data); unions (Table 7b) std::unordered_set 210 vs 0.270 on CensusInc (~778x, derived from page data). Membership queries (Table 6): Roaring beats std::vector + std::binary_search on every dataset (e.g. 63.6 vs 415 cycles on CensusInc), but std::unordered_set is faster than Roaring on CensusInc, CensusInc-sorted, Weather and Weather-sorted (e.g. 49.2 vs 63.6) and slower on Census1881 (38.2 vs 17.4). vs uncompressed bitset (cbitset): intersections 19.5 vs 0.090 on Census1881 (~217x, derived from page data), 33.0 vs 0.140 on Census1881-sorted (~236x, derived from page data), 26.4 vs 1.43 on Wikileaks (~18x, derived from page data); but on CensusInc/CensusInc-sorted/Weather the bitset is faster (CensusInc: bitset 0.120-0.130 vs Roaring 0.220-0.370 across the four set operations, ~1.7-3.1x, derived from page data). Bitset wins every membership query (2.36-3.74 vs Roaring 17.4-76.8 cycles). Memory (Table 4, bits/value): Roaring 15.1 vs bitset 524 on Census1881, 2.60 vs 5.66 on CensusInc, 0.340 vs 11.4 on Weather-sorted; std::vector uses 32 and std::unordered_set 195 bits/value on every dataset.
corrections.baseline: std::unordered_set<uint32_t> and sorted std::vector<uint32_t> with STL set algorithms (std::set_intersection/union/difference, std::binary_search) from the standard library bundled with GCC 5.4; also an uncompressed bitset (the authors' portable C 'cbitset', same word-array layout as std::bitset/std::vector<bool>)
corrections.caveats: Results depend heavily on dataset and operation: Roaring loses to a plain bitset on dense datasets and on all membership queries, and loses to std::unordered_set on membership queries for 4 of 8 datasets. The bitset baseline is the authors' own 'cbitset' C library, not std::bitset/std::vector<bool>. The STL containers are literally the standard library that ships with GCC 5.4 (libstdc++ inferred from 'the standard C++ library bundled with our compiler' on Linux), which is from 2016. The paper's authors also maintain the library (Lemire et al., Software: Practice and Experience 2018), but the code, compiler, flags and CPU are all public.

notes: Tier A stands. Downgraded because claimed_speedup mis-transcribed Table 4: Roaring on Census1881 uses 15.1 bits/value, not 2.60 (2.60 is CensusInc), so the memory win was overstated about 6x (~35x, not ~200x). Also the 0.380 in the CensusInc Roaring range belongs to BitMagic. Added the paper's direct libstdc++ std::vector/std::unordered_set comparisons, a stronger stdlib baseline than cbitset. License (Apache-2.0 OR MIT, from LICENSE since spdx=NOASSERTION), stars and last commit 2026-09-23 all confirmed.

tier_reason: plflib.org/bitsets.htm benchmarks plf::bitset against std::bitset under GCC 13.2 (nuwen mingw, libstdc++) and MSVC 2022 (MSVC STL), O2/AVX2/C++23 release, on an Intel i7-9750H. The benchmark code is public (plflib.org/plf_bitset_benchmarks_15-02-2025.zip, also in the repo root).

corrections.license: Computing For Good License v1.01 (non-OSI; zlib-style terms plus ethical field-of-use restrictions 4a-4e)
corrections.caveats: First-party benchmark (the author's own numbers), not independently reproduced, but methodology (compiler, flags, hardware) and full benchmark source are published. The extreme set_range/reset_range percentages (up to ~677x) mostly reflect that std::bitset has no ranged-set primitive (callers loop bit-by-bit), so they are partly an algorithmic win rather than a raw constant-factor speedup; the overall test-suite numbers (~20-24%) better represent general use. Not every operation wins: MSVC's std::bitset to_string (which uses an intrinsic) beats plf, and the author says other operations perform about the same. Licensed under 'Computing For Good License v1.01' (zlib-like with ethical-use restrictions 4a-4e, not OSI-approved), so usability is 'reference'.

notes: Every release and debug percentage in claimed_speedup matches the page (the page's summary lists left/right shift as 101%/35% and 98%/22% for GCC/MSVC; its body text says +35%/20% for MSVC, a small inconsistency on the page itself). The author states libc++ was not tested. Stars (14), last commit (2026-09-19) and non-fork status confirmed; the license field is filled from the LICENSE file (spdx=NOASSERTION).

tier_reason: First-party Google Benchmark code (benchmark/benchmark.cpp) and raw output (results.txt) are public, but no compiler, flags or CPU model are stated (the CMakeLists set no build type or optimization flags), so it cannot be A or B. The unstated flags plus a >50x gain would cap it at C anyway.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README claims 'improvements averaging 60x' versus the iterative std::bitset approach. benchmark/results.txt: N=8192: 953,294 ns (std::bitset .test(i) loop) vs 18,134 ns (better_bitset) = ~52.6x faster (derived from page data); N=1024: 128,450 vs 1,789 ns = ~71.8x (derived from page data); N=64: 6,349 vs 213 ns = ~29.8x (derived from page data); N=8: 701 vs 218 ns = ~3.2x (derived from page data); but N=4: 250 ns (std::bitset) vs 405 ns (better_bitset), so better_bitset is ~1.6x SLOWER there (derived from page data). The mean of the 13 per-size ratios is ~34x (derived from page data), below the README's 60x.
corrections.caveats: Small, unmaintained repo (last commit 2022, 8 stars). The benchmark is first-party and results.txt records no compiler or optimization flags (the CMakeLists set neither, so the build may not have been optimized), and names the CPU only by core count and clock speed. The std::bitset side is a naive bit-by-bit .test(i) loop written for the benchmark (standard std::bitset has no find-first operation; libstdc++'s non-standard _Find_first() was not used), so the speedup is mostly an algorithmic win over a strawman. better_bitset is slower at N=4. There is no LICENSE file, so the code can be studied but not safely reused.

notes: The numbers quoted in the record are correct, but it left out the N=4 loss, and the README's '60x average' is not supported by results.txt (mean per-size ratio ~34x, max ~72x). Metadata confirmed: no license, 8 stars, last commit 2022-04-08 (abandoned), not a fork.
